sessions.topic: Mitosis: how one cell becomes two

read.title: Mitosis: the copying machine inside you
read.intro: Every second, millions of your cells are splitting in two. Here's how — and why it has to be done perfectly.
body: You started life as a single cell, smaller than the full stop at the end of this sentence. Today your body is made of around 30 trillion cells. Every one of them came from that first cell, by a process of splitting in two, again and again and again. The type of cell division that builds and repairs your body is called **mitosis**, and it is happening inside you right now, millions of times a second.
## Why do cells need to divide?
There are three main reasons your body needs mitosis.

The first is **growth**. A baby does not grow by making its cells bigger. Cells have a size limit, because a cell that is too big cannot move food and oxygen in and waste out quickly enough. Instead, a growing body makes *more* cells. When you grow taller, it is because cells near the ends of your bones are dividing.

The second is **repair**. When you graze your knee, the cells around the wound divide to fill the gap. Within a week or two, new skin has replaced the damaged area. If you break a bone, mitosis builds new bone tissue to knit the pieces together.

The third is **replacement**. Many of your cells are worn out and replaced constantly. You lose tens of thousands of dead skin cells every minute; much of the dust in your house is actually old skin. The cells lining your stomach are replaced every few days, because stomach acid is so harsh. Your body makes millions of new blood cells every second, from special cells in your bone marrow that keep dividing.

Single-celled organisms, such as amoebas, use cell division in a different way: when an amoeba divides, it makes two complete new organisms. This is a kind of **asexual reproduction** — reproduction with only one parent.
## The instructions inside the nucleus

To understand mitosis, you need to know what is inside the **nucleus**, the control centre of the cell. The nucleus contains long threads called **chromosomes**. Each chromosome is made of a chemical called **DNA**, and along it are thousands of **genes**: sections of DNA that carry the instructions for making the body work, from your eye colour to the enzymes that digest your lunch.

Human body cells contain **46 chromosomes**, arranged in **23 pairs**. One chromosome in each pair came from your mother and one from your father. Every body cell — a skin cell, a muscle cell, a cell in your liver — has a full copy of these 46 chromosomes. This is crucial: if a new cell got the wrong number of chromosomes, it would have the wrong instructions, and it might not work properly or might die.
## The steps of mitosis
Mitosis has one job: to turn one cell into **two identical cells**, each with a complete set of 46 chromosomes. It happens in a set order.

**1. Copying.** Before the cell divides, it makes an exact copy of every chromosome. Each chromosome now consists of two identical strands joined in the middle, which gives chromosomes their famous X shape under a microscope. At this point, the cell is also growing and making more of the other parts it needs, such as mitochondria.
**2. Lining up.** The membrane around the nucleus breaks down, and the copied chromosomes line up across the middle of the cell.
**3. Pulling apart.** Tiny fibres attach to each chromosome and pull the two copies apart, so that one copy of every chromosome moves to each end of the cell.
**4. Two new nuclei.** A new membrane forms around each set of chromosomes, making two nuclei.
**5. Splitting.** Finally, the cytoplasm and cell membrane divide, pinching the cell in two. In plant cells, which have a rigid cell wall, a new wall forms down the middle instead.

The result is two **daughter cells**. Each has 46 chromosomes, and each is **genetically identical** to the original cell and to each other. Scientists call the whole repeating pattern of growing, copying and dividing the **cell cycle**.
## Seeing it for yourself

You can watch mitosis in a school laboratory using the tip of an onion root. Plants grow at the tips of their roots and shoots, where cells divide rapidly, so if you squash a root tip, stain it and look under a microscope, you can spot cells caught at different stages: some with chromosomes lined up in the middle, others being pulled apart. It is a little like looking at a photograph of a busy street and seeing people frozen mid-step.
## When mitosis goes wrong

Normally, mitosis is tightly controlled. Cells divide only when the body needs them to, and stop when the job is done. Sometimes, though, a cell's DNA becomes damaged — for example by ultraviolet light from the sun or by chemicals in cigarette smoke — and the cell starts dividing out of control. The growing lump of cells is called a **tumour**, and when it can invade other parts of the body, it is **cancer**. Many cancer treatments work by attacking cells that are dividing quickly, which is why they can also cause side effects such as hair loss: hair cells divide quickly too.
## The big picture

Mitosis is how one cell becomes a whole person, and how that person heals, grows and stays alive. It produces cells that are identical copies, which is exactly what the body needs for growth and repair. But identical copies are not always what living things need. In the next science session, you will meet **meiosis**, a different type of cell division that makes cells which are deliberately *not* identical — and discover why that makes every person unique.

keywords.def: Cell division that makes two genetically identical cells, used for growth, repair and replacement.
A long thread of DNA found in the nucleus, carrying many genes. Human body cells have 46.
A section of DNA that carries the instructions for one characteristic or protein.
The new cells produced when a cell divides.
The repeating pattern of a cell growing, copying its chromosomes and dividing.
A lump of cells formed when cell division gets out of control.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of mitosis in the human body?
options: To make sex cells such as sperm and eggs
To make new cells for growth, repair and replacement
questions.explain: Mitosis makes identical new cells so the body can grow, heal and replace worn-out cells. Sex cells are made by a different process, meiosis, which you'll meet next session.

questions.q: How many chromosomes are in a normal human body cell?
questions.explain: Human body cells have 46 chromosomes, arranged in 23 pairs — one of each pair from each parent.

questions.q: What are chromosomes made of?
questions.explain: Chromosomes are long threads of DNA. Sections of the DNA called genes carry instructions for the body.

questions.q: What happens first, before a cell divides by mitosis?
options: The cell loses half its chromosomes
questions.explain: The cell copies every chromosome first, so that there is a full set for each of the two new cells. That copying is why chromosomes look X-shaped just before division.

questions.q: A skin cell with 46 chromosomes divides by mitosis. How many chromosomes does each daughter cell have?
questions.explain: Mitosis makes identical copies, so each new cell has the full 46. A common mistake is to think the chromosomes are shared out in half — but they were copied first, so each cell gets a complete set.

questions.q: Why can't a growing body just make its existing cells bigger?
options: Cells are not allowed to change size
Bigger cells would have too many chromosomes
Bigger cells would be too heavy
A very big cell can't move food and oxygen in and waste out quickly enough
questions.explain: Substances have to travel across the cell membrane and through the cell. In a cell that is too big, this takes too long, so the body grows by making more cells instead.

questions.q: Why do scientists look at onion root tips to see mitosis?
options: Root tips grow quickly, so many cells there are dividing
questions.explain: Plants grow at the tips of roots and shoots, so lots of cells there are in the middle of dividing — ideal for spotting the different stages.

questions.q: What is a tumour?
options: A cell that has stopped dividing
A lump of cells formed when cell division gets out of control
questions.explain: If a cell's DNA is damaged, it may divide uncontrollably. The resulting lump is a tumour; if it spreads into other tissues, it is cancer.

questions.q: One cell divides by mitosis, then each new cell divides again, and so on. How many cells will there be after 5 rounds of division?
questions.explain: The number doubles each time: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 → 16 → 32. That's 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32. Doubling is why cell numbers can grow so quickly.

questions.q: Recap from last week: why are saucepans made of metal?
options: Metals are good conductors of heat
Metals are good conductors of electricity
questions.explain: A saucepan needs to carry heat from the hob to the food, so it's about conducting heat (thermal conduction). Metals also conduct electricity — but that's why we use them in wires, not pans. The handle is a non-metal because non-metals are poor conductors of heat.

reflect: Explain why your body needs mitosis. Give two different examples of it happening.
A friend says: 'When a cell divides by mitosis, each new cell gets half the chromosomes.' Explain what's wrong with this.

read.title: Brazil: one country, many worlds
read.intro: Rainforest and skyscrapers, great wealth and deep poverty: meet the giant of South America.
body: Brazil is enormous. It covers almost half of South America and is the fifth-largest country in the world by area — big enough to fit the UK inside it about 35 times. More than 200 million people live there, making it one of the most populated countries on Earth. It has the largest part of the Amazon rainforest, some of the world's biggest cities, and one of the largest economies in the world. Yet it also has some of the sharpest differences between rich and poor you will find anywhere. Geographers often describe it as a **country of contrasts**.
## A short history

Before Europeans arrived, Brazil was home to millions of **indigenous** people, living in hundreds of different groups. In 1500, Portuguese explorers landed on the coast and claimed the land for Portugal. That is why Brazilians speak **Portuguese**, not Spanish like most of their neighbours. The Portuguese set up huge sugar plantations along the north-east coast and forced around 4 to 5 million enslaved Africans across the Atlantic to work on them — more than any other country in the Americas. Brazil was also the last country in the Americas to abolish slavery, in 1888. Brazil became independent in 1822. Today its population is one of the most diverse in the world, with indigenous, European, African and Asian roots.
## Five regions, five different worlds
Brazil is usually divided into five regions, and they could hardly be more different.

The **North** is mostly covered by the **Amazon rainforest**. It is the largest region but has the fewest people, many of them living along the rivers. The Amazon River carries more water than any other river on Earth.

The **Northeast** was the first area the Portuguese settled. Its coast has beautiful beaches and historic cities such as Salvador, but inland is the **sertão**, a hot, dry area that suffers long droughts. The Northeast is the poorest region, and for decades millions of people have left it to look for work in the cities further south.

The **Southeast** is Brazil's economic heart. It contains **São Paulo**, the largest city in South America, with over 20 million people in its wider area, and **Rio de Janeiro**, famous for its beaches, its carnival and its favelas. Most of Brazil's factories, banks and big companies are here, and average incomes are more than double those in the Northeast.
The **South** is cooler, with a climate closer to Europe's. Many people here are descended from Italian and German immigrants, and the region is known for its farms and well-paid industries.

The **Centre-West** is a vast area of tropical grassland called the **cerrado**, which has been turned into huge farms growing soya beans and raising cattle. It is also home to **Brasília**, the capital. Brasília was built from scratch in the 1950s and opened in 1960 to encourage people and businesses to move inland, away from the crowded coast. From the air, its central plan looks like an aeroplane.
## How developed is Brazil?
Brazil is a **newly emerging economy** (NEE). It is not as wealthy as high-income countries like the UK, but its economy has grown quickly and it is far richer than low-income countries.

Look at the indicators. Brazil's **GNI per capita** is around $9,000 a year, compared with around $49,000 in the UK and only a few hundred dollars in the poorest countries. Life expectancy is about 76 years, only a few years less than in the UK. Its HDI is just under 0.8, which the United Nations counts as 'high' human development.

Brazil's economy is varied. It is the world's largest producer of **coffee** and the largest exporter of **soya beans**. It exports huge amounts of iron ore, oil, beef, sugar and orange juice. But it also makes cars and aircraft: Embraer, a Brazilian company, is one of the world's biggest makers of passenger jets.
## A deeply unequal country

The figures above are national averages, and as you learned last week, averages can hide a lot. Brazil is one of the most **unequal** countries in the world. The richest tenth of the population receives around 40% of all the income, while millions of people live in poverty. In cities like Rio and São Paulo, luxury apartment blocks with swimming pools can stand within sight of crowded informal settlements called **favelas**, where homes may lack proper sewers or safe electricity.

Inequality also follows the regions. A child born in the Southeast is likely to have better schools, healthcare and job chances than a child born in the rural Northeast. Indigenous peoples, and many Black Brazilians, still face discrimination and poverty.
## Fighting poverty

Brazil has tried hard to close these gaps. In 2003 the government launched **Bolsa Família**, which gives poor families a small monthly payment — on condition that their children go to school and get vaccinated. It is one of the largest programmes of its kind in the world. Supporters say it has helped lift millions of people out of extreme poverty and kept children in education, though critics argue it does not tackle the deeper causes of poverty, such as low wages and poor housing.
## Why Brazil matters

Brazil shows that development is not a simple ladder that every country climbs in the same way. It is a country where world-class companies and some of the most advanced farming on Earth exist alongside favelas and drought-hit villages. Over the next sessions you will zoom in on two of its most famous places: the city of **Rio de Janeiro**, and the **Amazon rainforest**.

keywords.def: Newly emerging economy: a country whose economy is growing quickly, between low- and high-income, e.g. Brazil.
Gross national income per person: the total income of a country's people in a year, divided by its population.
Belonging to the people who lived in a place first, before outsiders arrived.
Big differences in wealth or opportunities between different groups of people.
An informal settlement in a Brazilian city, often built by residents on land they don't own.
The hot, dry inland area of north-east Brazil, which suffers from drought.

questions.q: Why do most Brazilians speak Portuguese?
options: Portuguese is the easiest language to learn
Brazil was colonised by Portugal from 1500
It was chosen by vote in 1960
questions.explain: Portuguese explorers claimed Brazil in 1500, and it was a Portuguese colony until independence in 1822. Most of its neighbours were colonised by Spain.

questions.q: Which is Brazil's poorest region, affected by drought inland?
questions.explain: The Northeast includes the dry sertão, which suffers long droughts. It is the poorest region, and many people have migrated from it to cities in the Southeast.

questions.q: What is the capital city of Brazil?
questions.explain: Brasília was purpose-built inland and became the capital in 1960, taking over from Rio de Janeiro. São Paulo is the biggest city, but not the capital.

questions.q: Why is Brazil classed as an NEE (newly emerging economy)?
options: It has the lowest GNI per capita in the world
Its economy is growing quickly and it sits between low- and high-income countries
It is in the southern hemisphere
questions.explain: NEEs are countries whose economies have grown fast but which are not yet as wealthy as HICs. Brazil's GNI per capita (around $9,000) is well above LICs but well below the UK.

questions.q: Brazil's HDI is just under 0.8. What does this suggest?
options: Life in Brazil is identical to life in the UK
Brazil has very low life expectancy
Brazil has the highest HDI in the world
Most people have reasonably good health, education and income, though not as high as in the richest countries
questions.explain: An HDI close to 0.8 counts as 'high' development. It's below the UK's (about 0.94), but far above the lowest countries (around 0.4).

questions.q: Brazil's average figures look quite good, yet millions of Brazilians live in poverty. Why?
options: The averages hide very large inequality between rich and poor
Poor people aren't counted in the figures
Brazil's figures are measured in a different currency
questions.explain: Brazil is one of the most unequal countries in the world. The richest tenth receive around 40% of all income, so a decent average can hide great poverty — just like the GNI point you made last week.

questions.q: How does Bolsa Família try to reduce poverty?
options: It builds new cities in the rainforest
It pays poor families a monthly sum if their children attend school and get vaccinated
It gives free land to every family
It bans people from moving to cities
questions.explain: Bolsa Família is a 'conditional cash transfer': families get money, and in return children go to school and get vaccinated. It tackles poverty now and invests in children's futures.

questions.q: Which of these does NOT fit Brazil's economy?
options: Major exporter of soya beans and iron ore
Its economy depends only on one crop
questions.explain: Brazil's economy is varied: farming, mining, oil and manufacturing (including aircraft). That variety is one reason it is an NEE rather than an LIC dependent on one export.

questions.q: GNI per capita is around $49,000 in the UK and around $9,000 in Brazil. Roughly how many times larger is the UK's?
questions.explain: 49,000 ÷ 9,000 ≈ 5.4, so about 5 times. Compare that with Niger (around 80 times smaller than the UK) and you can see why Brazil is an NEE, not an LIC.

questions.q: Brazil's area is about 8.5 million km² and the UK's is about 0.24 million km². About how many times bigger is Brazil?
questions.explain: 8.5 ÷ 0.24 ≈ 35. You could fit the UK inside Brazil about 35 times.

reflect: Brazil is often called a 'country of contrasts'. Give two examples from the article that show why.
Using two development indicators, explain why Brazil is an NEE rather than an HIC or an LIC.

sessions.topic: Meiosis: why no two people are the same

read.title: Meiosis: the shuffle that makes you unique
read.intro: Mitosis makes identical copies. Meiosis does the opposite — on purpose.
body: Look around your family. You might have your mum's eyes, your dad's laugh and your grandmother's curly hair. If you have brothers or sisters, you probably share some features with them, but you are certainly not identical. Why not? You all have the same two parents. The answer lies in a special kind of cell division called **meiosis**, which shuffles genes like a pack of cards every time a new sex cell is made.
## A problem with numbers

Humans, like most animals and plants, reproduce by **sexual reproduction**. A sex cell from the father (a **sperm** cell) joins with a sex cell from the mother (an **egg** cell). This joining is called **fertilisation**, and it produces a single new cell — the first cell of a new person. Sex cells have a special name: **gametes**.

Now think about chromosomes. You know from mitosis that normal human body cells contain **46 chromosomes**. Imagine if sperm and eggs were made by mitosis, so that they also had 46 each. When they joined at fertilisation, the new cell would have 92 chromosomes. In the next generation it would be 184, then 368, doubling every time. That would be a disaster: the instructions in the cell would be hopelessly muddled.

Meiosis solves this problem. It makes gametes that contain only **half** the normal number of chromosomes: **23** in humans, one from each pair. When a sperm with 23 chromosomes fertilises an egg with 23 chromosomes, the new cell has 23 + 23 = 46. The right number is restored, and the new cell can then grow into a baby by mitosis.
## Where and how meiosis happens

Meiosis takes place only in the reproductive organs: in the **testes**, which make sperm, and the **ovaries**, which make eggs. In flowering plants, it happens in the **anthers**, which make pollen, and the **ovules**, which contain the plant's egg cells. Everywhere else in the body, cells divide by mitosis.

Like mitosis, meiosis begins with the cell copying all its chromosomes. But then something different happens. The chromosomes line up in their **pairs** — your mother's chromosome 1 next to your father's chromosome 1, and so on — and the cell divides **twice**, not once.

In the first division, the pairs are separated, so each new cell gets one chromosome from each pair. In the second division, the copies are pulled apart, just as in mitosis. The result is **four cells**, each with **23 chromosomes**, and — crucially — each one **genetically different** from the others and from the parent cell.
## The great shuffle
Why are the four cells different? There are two main reasons.

The first is **random sorting**. When the pairs line up and separate, it is pure chance which chromosome from each pair goes into which cell. Think of it like tossing a coin for each of your 23 pairs: heads, the gamete gets the chromosome you inherited from your mum; tails, it gets the one from your dad. With 23 coin tosses, the number of possible combinations is 2 multiplied by itself 23 times — more than **8 million** different combinations from one person.

The second is **crossing over**. While the pairs are lined up side by side, they can swap sections of DNA with each other. This creates brand-new combinations of genes on each chromosome — combinations that never existed before.

Put those together, then remember that a baby is made from *two* gametes, one from each parent, and the number of possible genetic combinations becomes astronomically large. That's why, apart from identical twins, no two people who have ever lived have had exactly the same DNA.
## What about identical twins?

Identical twins are the exception that proves the rule. They form when a single fertilised egg divides by mitosis into two cells, and those two cells separate and grow into two babies. Because mitosis makes identical copies, the twins have the same DNA. Non-identical twins are different: they come from two separate eggs fertilised by two separate sperm, so they are no more alike genetically than any other brothers and sisters.
## Boy or girl?

Meiosis also explains why roughly half of babies are boys and half are girls. One of your 23 pairs is the **sex chromosomes**. Females usually have two X chromosomes (XX); males usually have one X and one Y (XY). When eggs are made by meiosis, every egg gets an X. When sperm are made, half get an X and half get a Y. So whether a baby is a boy or a girl depends on which kind of sperm fertilises the egg — a 50:50 chance each time.
## Mitosis and meiosis side by side

It is easy to mix the two up, so here is a summary. **Mitosis** happens all over the body; it involves one division; it makes **two** cells; they have the **full number** of chromosomes (46); and they are **identical**. Its job is growth and repair. **Meiosis** happens only in reproductive organs; it involves two divisions; it makes **four** cells; they have **half** the number of chromosomes (23); and they are all **different**. Its job is to make gametes for sexual reproduction. A memory trick: mi**t**osis makes **t**wo (both have a 't'), while **me**iosis is how you got to be **me** — a unique person.
## Why variation matters

Meiosis creates **variation**: differences between individuals of the same species. That might sound like a happy accident, but it is hugely important. If a disease sweeps through a population, or the climate changes, variation means that some individuals are likely to have features that help them survive. They pass on their genes, and the species carries on. Later this week, you will see how this variation is the raw material for **evolution** — the process that has shaped every living thing on Earth.

keywords.def: Cell division that makes four genetically different gametes, each with half the normal number of chromosomes.
A sex cell: sperm or egg in animals; pollen or egg cells in plants.
When the nucleus of a male gamete joins with the nucleus of a female gamete.
When a pair of chromosomes swap sections of DNA during meiosis, creating new combinations of genes.
The pair that decides sex: usually XX in females and XY in males.
Differences between individuals of the same species.

questions.q: What does meiosis produce?
options: Gametes (sex cells) that are genetically different
questions.explain: Meiosis makes four gametes, each with half the chromosomes and each genetically different. Two identical cells is mitosis.

questions.q: How many chromosomes are in a human sperm or egg cell?
questions.explain: Gametes have half the normal number: 23. When sperm and egg join, 23 + 23 = 46, the normal number for a body cell.

questions.q: Where does meiosis take place in humans?
options: In every cell of the body
questions.explain: Meiosis only happens in reproductive organs, which make gametes. Everywhere else, cells divide by mitosis.

questions.q: Why must gametes have half the normal number of chromosomes?
options: So that they can swim faster
Because they are smaller than other cells
So that fertilisation restores the normal number, rather than doubling it
Because half the chromosomes are damaged
questions.explain: If gametes had 46 chromosomes, the fertilised egg would have 92, and the number would double every generation. Halving then joining keeps it at 46.

questions.q: A dog's body cells have 78 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are in a dog's sperm cell?
questions.explain: Gametes have half the body-cell number: 78 ÷ 2 = 39. (23 is the human number — different species have different numbers.)

questions.q: Which of these makes the cells produced by meiosis genetically different from each other?
options: The cells copying their DNA exactly
Chromosome pairs being sorted randomly, and crossing over
The cells being made in the skin
questions.explain: Random sorting of chromosome pairs, plus crossing over (swapping sections of DNA), mixes up the genes in each gamete. That's why each one is unique.

questions.q: Why are identical twins genetically identical?
options: They come from two eggs fertilised by the same sperm
They were born on the same day
They come from two eggs and two sperm
They come from one fertilised egg that split in two by mitosis
questions.explain: Identical twins come from a single fertilised egg that splits into two by mitosis, which makes identical copies. Non-identical twins come from two separate eggs and two separate sperm.

questions.q: A baby's sex is decided by:
options: The egg, because eggs carry either X or Y
The time of year it is born
Whether the sperm that fertilises the egg carries an X or a Y chromosome
How many chromosomes the egg has
questions.explain: Every egg carries an X. Half of sperm carry an X (making a girl, XX) and half carry a Y (making a boy, XY). So it's the sperm that decides, with a 50:50 chance.

questions.q: Which row correctly describes mitosis compared with meiosis?
options: Mitosis: 4 different cells; meiosis: 2 identical cells
Mitosis: 2 identical cells; meiosis: 4 different cells
questions.explain: Mitosis — two identical cells with the full number of chromosomes (growth and repair). Meiosis — four different cells with half the number (gametes).

questions.q: Fruit flies have 4 pairs of chromosomes. With random sorting, the number of combinations in one gamete is 2 × 2 × 2 × 2. How many is that?
questions.explain: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16. For humans, with 23 pairs, it's 2 multiplied by itself 23 times — over 8 million — and that's before crossing over adds even more.

reflect: Explain why sperm and egg cells must have only half the normal number of chromosomes. Use numbers in your answer.
Explain why you and a brother, sister or cousin look different, even though you share family. Use the words 'meiosis' and 'variation'.

read.title: Finding x: how to solve equations
read.intro: Grab a pencil and some paper if you can — this one is best done by working through the examples.
body: Algebra can look scary because of the letters, but finding x is really just solving a puzzle. Someone has hidden a number, and the equation gives you clues to find it. Once you know the rules, every equation can be solved the same way, step by step. By the end of this article you should be able to solve any of the types of equation you'll meet in Year 8.
## What is an equation?

An **equation** is a statement that two things are equal. The equals sign means 'is the same as'. For example, x + 3 = 10 means 'some number, plus 3, is the same as 10'. The letter x is called the **unknown** or the **variable**. To **solve** the equation means to find the value of x that makes the statement true. Here, x = 7, because 7 + 3 = 10.
## The balance idea

The best way to think about an equation is as a set of old-fashioned **balance scales**. Whatever is on the left side weighs exactly the same as whatever is on the right. If you take something off one side, the scales tip — unless you take exactly the same thing off the other side. So the golden rule of solving equations is:
**Whatever you do to one side, you must do to the other side.**
As long as you follow that rule, the equation stays balanced and stays true. Your aim is to get x on its own on one side.
## Undoing with inverse operations

To get x on its own, you **undo** whatever has been done to it, using **inverse operations** (opposites). Adding is undone by subtracting. Subtracting is undone by adding. Multiplying is undone by dividing. Dividing is undone by multiplying.
**Example 1:** x + 9 = 23. Something has been added to x (9), so subtract 9 from both sides: x = 23 − 9, so **x = 14**.
**Example 2:** 4x = 36. Remember, 4x means 4 × x. To undo multiplying by 4, divide both sides by 4: x = 36 ÷ 4, so **x = 9**.
**Example 3:** x ÷ 5 = 6 (often written as a fraction, x over 5). To undo dividing by 5, multiply both sides by 5: **x = 30**.
## Two-step equations

Many equations need two steps. Take 3x + 4 = 19. Think about what has happened to x: first it was multiplied by 3, then 4 was added. To undo it, work **backwards**, like taking off your shoes before your socks: undo the adding first, then the multiplying.
Step 1: subtract 4 from both sides. 3x = 15.
Step 2: divide both sides by 3. **x = 5**.

Now **check** by putting your answer back into the original equation. This is called **substitution**: 3 × 5 + 4 = 15 + 4 = 19. ✓ It works. Checking takes ten seconds and catches most mistakes, so make it a habit.
Another one: 5x − 7 = 18. Add 7 to both sides: 5x = 25. Divide by 5: **x = 5**. Check: 5 × 5 − 7 = 25 − 7 = 18 ✓.
## Unknowns on both sides

Sometimes x appears on both sides, as in 5x − 7 = 2x + 8. The trick is to collect all the x terms on one side first. Subtract 2x from both sides (the balance rule!): 3x − 7 = 8. Now it's a normal two-step equation. Add 7: 3x = 15. Divide by 3: **x = 5**. Check: left side 5 × 5 − 7 = 18; right side 2 × 5 + 8 = 18 ✓.
Tip: move the *smaller* number of x's, so you don't end up with negative x's.
## Equations with brackets

For an equation like 2(x + 3) = 18, you have two options. You can **expand** the brackets first, multiplying everything inside by 2: 2x + 6 = 18. Then subtract 6: 2x = 12. Divide by 2: **x = 6**. Or, because 2 lots of (x + 3) make 18, you can divide both sides by 2 straight away: x + 3 = 9, so x = 6. Both methods give the same answer, which is a nice way to check.
## Writing your own equations
In exams, word problems ask you to **form** an equation yourself. The key is to call the unknown number x (or n) and translate the words into maths, step by step.

'I think of a number. I multiply it by 4 and subtract 6. The answer is 30.' Let the number be n. Multiply by 4: 4n. Subtract 6: 4n − 6. The answer is 30: **4n − 6 = 30**. Now solve: add 6 to get 4n = 36, then divide by 4: **n = 9**.

Shapes work the same way. A rectangle is x cm wide and (x + 5) cm long, and its perimeter is 34 cm. The perimeter is all four sides added up: x + x + (x + 5) + (x + 5) = 34, which simplifies to 4x + 10 = 34. Subtract 10: 4x = 24. Divide by 4: **x = 6**. So the rectangle is 6 cm wide and 11 cm long. Check: 6 + 6 + 11 + 11 = 34 ✓.
## Common mistakes

The most common mistake is only doing something to one side. The second is undoing steps in the wrong order: in 3x + 4 = 19, dividing by 3 first is possible but messy, because you'd have to divide the 4 as well. The third is a sign slip: in x − 8 = 12, you **add** 8 (x = 20), not subtract. Write each step on a new line, keep the equals signs lined up, and always check your answer by substituting it back in.

keywords.def: A statement that two expressions are equal, e.g. 3x + 4 = 19.
A letter that stands for a number you need to find.
Find the value of the unknown that makes the equation true.
The opposite operation that undoes another: + and −, × and ÷.
Putting a number in place of a letter — used to check your answer.
Multiply out brackets, e.g. 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6.

questions.q: Solve: x + 9 = 23
questions.explain: Subtract 9 from both sides: x = 23 − 9 = 14. Check: 14 + 9 = 23 ✓. (32 comes from adding instead of subtracting.)

questions.q: Solve: 6x = 42
questions.explain: 6x means 6 × x, so divide both sides by 6: x = 42 ÷ 6 = 7. Check: 6 × 7 = 42 ✓.

questions.q: Solve: x ÷ 4 = 9
questions.explain: To undo dividing by 4, multiply both sides by 4: x = 9 × 4 = 36. Check: 36 ÷ 4 = 9 ✓.

questions.q: Solve: 2x + 5 = 17
questions.explain: Subtract 5 first: 2x = 12. Then divide by 2: x = 6. Check: 2 × 6 + 5 = 17 ✓. (8.5 comes from dividing 17 by 2 before dealing with the + 5.)

questions.q: What should be the first step to solve 3x − 4 = 20?
options: Divide only the left side by 3
questions.explain: Undo the − 4 first by adding 4 to both sides: 3x = 24. Then divide by 3: x = 8. Work backwards: last thing done, first thing undone.

questions.q: Sam says x = 3 is the solution to 4x + 1 = 15. Is Sam right?
options: No, because the answer should be negative
questions.explain: Substitute x = 3: 4 × 3 + 1 = 12 + 1 = 13, not 15, so Sam is wrong. The correct answer is x = 3.5 (4x = 14, so x = 14 ÷ 4). Checking catches mistakes like this.

questions.q: Solve: 7x − 3 = 4x + 9
questions.explain: Subtract 4x from both sides: 3x − 3 = 9. Add 3: 3x = 12. Divide by 3: x = 4. Check: 7 × 4 − 3 = 25 and 4 × 4 + 9 = 25 ✓.

questions.q: Solve: 3(x − 2) = 21
questions.explain: Divide both sides by 3: x − 2 = 7, so x = 9. Or expand: 3x − 6 = 21, 3x = 27, x = 9. Check: 3 × (9 − 2) = 3 × 7 = 21 ✓.

questions.q: 'I think of a number, multiply it by 5 and add 8. The answer is 43.' What is the number?
questions.explain: Form the equation: 5n + 8 = 43. Subtract 8: 5n = 35. Divide by 5: n = 7. Check: 5 × 7 + 8 = 43 ✓.

questions.q: A rectangle is x cm wide and (x + 3) cm long. Its perimeter is 26 cm. What is x?
questions.explain: Perimeter = x + x + (x + 3) + (x + 3) = 4x + 6. So 4x + 6 = 26, 4x = 20, x = 5. The rectangle is 5 cm by 8 cm, and 5 + 5 + 8 + 8 = 26 ✓.

reflect: Explain, step by step in words, how to solve 5x + 3 = 28. Say what you do to both sides at each step, and how you'd check your answer.
Make up your own 'I think of a number' puzzle. Write it as an equation, then solve it, showing each step.

sessions.subject: Geography
sessions.topic: Rio de Janeiro and its favelas

read.title: Rio de Janeiro: a city on the hillsides
read.intro: Why did millions of people move to Rio — and what is life like in the favelas they built?
body: Rio de Janeiro is one of the most recognisable cities on Earth. Picture Copacabana beach, the giant statue of Christ the Redeemer with its arms outstretched above the city, and Sugarloaf Mountain rising out of the bay. Rio hosted the football World Cup final in 2014 and the Olympic Games in 2016. But look up from the beaches at the steep green hills behind them and you will see something else: thousands of brick homes stacked on top of each other, climbing the slopes. These are Rio's **favelas**, and around one in five of the city's 6 million people live in them.
## A city that grew too fast

In 1950, most Brazilians lived in the countryside. Today, almost nine out of ten live in towns and cities. This growth in the proportion of people living in urban areas is called **urbanisation**, and in Brazil it happened at astonishing speed. Rio's population more than doubled in the second half of the twentieth century.

Cities grow in two ways. The first is **natural increase**: more babies are born than people die. In Rio, many migrants were young adults, so they had children in the city, adding to the growth. The second is **rural–urban migration**: people moving from the countryside to the city. Geographers explain migration using **push factors**, which drive people away from where they live, and **pull factors**, which attract them to a new place.

For millions of people in Brazil's poor, drought-hit Northeast, the push factors were strong. Long droughts in the sertão destroyed crops and livestock. Big landowners held most of the land, so many families had none of their own. Farms were becoming mechanised, so fewer workers were needed. Schools and health care were poor, and there were few jobs.

Rio's pull factors were just as powerful: the hope of a job in a factory, on a building site or in someone's home; better schools for children; hospitals; electricity; entertainment; and the stories of friends and relatives who had already made the move. Not everyone found the life they hoped for, but for many, the city still offered more chances than the countryside.
## Building a home with your own hands

When millions of migrants arrived, there was nowhere near enough housing, and what existed was far too expensive. So people built their own. They found empty land that nobody was using — often steep hillsides, swampy ground or land beside motorways — and put up shacks of wood and metal sheets. These **informal settlements** became the favelas. Because residents did not own the land, they could be evicted, and the city did not provide services like water pipes, sewers or rubbish collection.

Over the decades, the favelas changed. Families saved up and gradually replaced their shacks with brick and concrete, adding extra floors when they could afford it. Today, many favelas are permanent neighbourhoods, with shops, cafés, churches, schools and football pitches. **Rocinha**, Rio's largest favela, is officially home to around 70,000 people, though some estimates put it at twice that. It is almost a city in its own right.
## Life in the favelas

Life in a favela can be hard. Many homes are overcrowded, with a whole family in one or two rooms. Some areas still lack proper sewers, so waste runs in open channels, spreading diseases. Electricity may be taken illegally from overhead cables, which is dangerous. Homes built on steep slopes are at risk of **landslides** after heavy rain, and these have killed people in Rio. Many residents work in the **informal economy** — jobs such as street selling, cleaning or delivery, which are not officially registered — so they have no guaranteed wage, sick pay or pension. Some favelas are controlled by drug gangs, and violence between gangs and police is a serious problem.

But it would be wrong to see favelas only as places of problems. They are lively communities where neighbours know each other and help each other out. Residents have built their homes themselves, and many run small businesses. Favelas have produced famous musicians, dancers and footballers. And because they are close to the city centre and the rich neighbourhoods by the beaches, residents can reach jobs more easily than people who live on the city's outer edges.
## A divided city

Rio shows inequality in a way you can see with your own eyes. Rocinha's homes look down on São Conrado, a neighbourhood of luxury flats and a golf course. People from the favelas may clean the flats, guard the buildings and cook in the restaurants of wealthy areas, yet live with far fewer services themselves.
## Can the favelas be improved?

Rio has tried several approaches. In the past, the authorities sometimes simply bulldozed favelas and moved residents to new housing estates far from the centre. This often failed: people lost their homes, communities were broken up, and the new estates were hours away from work.

From the 1990s, the city tried a different approach: **upgrading** favelas rather than destroying them. A programme called **Favela-Bairro** (meaning 'favela to neighbourhood') paved streets, laid water and sewage pipes, built community centres and nurseries, and gave some residents legal rights to their land. **Self-help schemes** gave people materials to improve their own homes. Some favelas received new transport links, such as a cable car over the Complexo do Alemão, which opened in 2011 — though it was closed a few years later after money ran out.

Before the 2014 World Cup and 2016 Olympics, the government also sent special police units into some favelas to drive out drug gangs. At first, violence fell in some areas, but critics say the improvements did not last and that residents were not properly involved in decisions about their own neighbourhoods.
## What can we learn?

Rio's story shows the challenges facing fast-growing cities across the world, from Mumbai to Lagos. Rapid urbanisation brings opportunities, such as jobs and services, as well as serious problems. Most geographers now agree that the best solutions work *with* residents, improving the places where they already live, rather than simply clearing them away.

keywords.def: An increase in the proportion of people living in towns and cities.
People moving from the countryside to towns and cities.
Something that makes people want to leave a place, e.g. drought or lack of jobs.
Something that attracts people to a place, e.g. jobs, schools or hospitals.
Housing built by residents on land they don't legally own, without official services.
Work that isn't officially registered or taxed, e.g. street selling, with no guaranteed wage.

questions.q: What is urbanisation?
options: Building new roads in the countryside
People moving from cities to villages
An increase in the proportion of people living in towns and cities
questions.explain: Urbanisation is about the share of a country's population living in urban areas going up. In Brazil it has risen to almost 9 in 10 people.

questions.q: Which of these is a push factor that made people leave north-east Brazil?
options: Friends who had already moved to Rio
questions.explain: Push factors drive people away. Drought in the sertão destroyed crops and incomes. The other three are pull factors that attract people to the city.

questions.q: Which of these is a pull factor attracting people to Rio?
options: The chance of a job and better schools
Big landowners owning most of the land
Poor health care in the countryside
questions.explain: Pull factors attract people to a place. Jobs and schools in Rio drew people in; the other options are reasons for leaving the countryside (push factors).

questions.q: Why did migrants build favelas on steep hillsides and swampy land?
options: Because the government ordered them to
Because the land was the safest in the city
Because it was empty land that nobody else was using, and they couldn't afford housing
questions.explain: There wasn't enough affordable housing, so people built on unused land — often unused precisely because it was steep or wet. That's why some favelas face landslide and flood risks.

questions.q: What is the informal economy?
options: Work that isn't officially registered, such as street selling, with no guaranteed wage
Jobs that only happen at weekends
questions.explain: Informal jobs aren't registered or taxed, so workers have no contract, sick pay or pension. Many favela residents earn a living this way.

questions.q: What did the Favela-Bairro programme do?
options: Upgraded favelas with paved streets, water pipes, sewers and community centres
Moved all favela residents to the countryside
questions.explain: Favela-Bairro ('favela to neighbourhood') improved favelas where they stood, rather than destroying them — keeping communities together near their jobs.

questions.q: Why did moving favela residents to new estates far from the centre often fail?
options: The new homes were too big
Communities were broken up and the estates were far from people's jobs
The new estates were too close to the beach
questions.explain: Favelas may be poor, but they're close to work. Moving people far away meant long, expensive journeys and the loss of the neighbours and networks people relied on.

questions.q: Which of these is a positive feature of many favelas?
options: Strong communities where neighbours help each other
questions.explain: Favelas face real problems, but they are also lively communities with businesses, culture and strong support networks. Good geography answers show both sides.

questions.q: About 6 million people live in Rio, and around one in five live in favelas. Roughly how many is that?
questions.explain: One in five means divide by 5: 6 million ÷ 5 = 1.2 million. That's more than the whole population of Birmingham.

questions.q: In 1950, about 1 in 3 Brazilians lived in towns and cities. Today it's almost 9 in 10. What does this show?
options: Most Brazilians now live in the Amazon
questions.explain: The share of people living in urban areas has risen from about a third to almost nine-tenths — that's rapid urbanisation, driven by rural–urban migration and natural increase.

reflect: Give one push factor and one pull factor that brought migrants to Rio. Explain how each one affected people's decision to move.
Is it better to upgrade favelas where they are, or to knock them down and build new flats further away? Give your view and explain why.

sessions.subject: French
sessions.topic: At the café, and what's in your town

read.title: Au café et en ville: ordering and describing your town
read.intro: Read the French phrases out loud in your head as you go — it really helps them stick.
body: Imagine you are on holiday in France. It is a warm morning, you have just walked round the market, and you sit down at a table outside a café. A waiter comes over. What do you say? And later, when your French penfriend asks what there is to do in your town, how do you answer? This session gives you the key phrases for both — and the grammar that holds them together.
## Café culture

Cafés are a big part of everyday life in France. People meet friends there, read the newspaper, or simply sit and watch the world go by. Many cafés have tables outside on the pavement, called the **terrasse**. One important tip: in France, it is polite to say **Bonjour** when you walk into a café or shop, and **Au revoir** when you leave. Saying nothing can seem rude. When you speak to a waiter, use **vous**, the polite form of 'you', rather than **tu**, which is for friends, family and children.
## Ordering
The waiter might start with *Bonjour, vous désirez ?* ('Hello, what would you like?') or *Qu'est-ce que vous voulez boire ?* ('What would you like to drink?').

The most useful phrase for ordering is **Je voudrais…** which means 'I would like…'. It is polite and works for anything: *Je voudrais un chocolat chaud, s'il vous plaît* ('I would like a hot chocolate, please'). You can also say **Je vais prendre…** ('I'm going to have…') or, more casually, **Pour moi…** ('For me…'). Always finish with **s'il vous plaît** ('please').

Here are some drinks: *un café* (a coffee — in France, this usually means a small, strong espresso), *un thé* (a tea), *un chocolat chaud* (a hot chocolate), *un jus d'orange* (an orange juice), *une limonade* (a lemonade), *un coca* (a cola) and *une eau minérale* (a mineral water).

And some food: *un croissant*, *un pain au chocolat*, *une crêpe* (a thin pancake), *un croque-monsieur* (a toasted ham and cheese sandwich), *une glace* (an ice cream), *une omelette* and *un sandwich au fromage* (a cheese sandwich).

The waiter may then ask *Et avec ça ?* ('And with that?') or *C'est tout ?* ('Is that everything?'). You can answer *Oui, c'est tout, merci* ('Yes, that's all, thanks'). When you want to pay, say **L'addition, s'il vous plaît** ('The bill, please') or ask **C'est combien ?** ('How much is it?'). Prices are in euros: *trois euros cinquante* means €3.50.
## Un or une?

You will have noticed that some words have **un** and some have **une**. Both mean 'a' or 'an', but French nouns are either **masculine** or **feminine**. Masculine nouns take *un* (*un café*, *un croissant*) and feminine nouns take *une* (*une crêpe*, *une limonade*). There is not always a logical reason, so the best way is to learn each noun together with its *un* or *une*, as if they were one word. The words for 'the' work the same way: **le** for masculine (*le café*) and **la** for feminine (*la crêpe*). Before a vowel, both shorten to **l'** (*l'addition*, *l'omelette*), and in the plural, both become **les**.
## Describing your town

When someone asks *Qu'est-ce qu'il y a dans ta ville ?* ('What is there in your town?'), the key phrase is **Il y a…** which means both 'there is' and 'there are'. *Dans ma ville, il y a un cinéma et une piscine* ('In my town, there is a cinema and a swimming pool').

Useful places: *un cinéma*, *un parc*, *un marché* (a market), *un musée* (a museum), *un stade* (a stadium), *un centre commercial* (a shopping centre), *un château* (a castle), *une piscine* (a swimming pool), *une bibliothèque* (a library — not a bookshop, which is *une librairie*!), *une gare* (a train station), *une église* (a church), *une patinoire* (an ice rink), and *des magasins* (some shops). *Des* means 'some' and is used for plural nouns.
## Saying what there isn't

To say there isn't something, wrap **ne… pas** around the verb: *il n'y a pas*. But here's the rule that catches lots of people out: after a negative, *un*, *une* and *des* all change to **de** (or **d'** before a vowel). So: *Il y a un cinéma* becomes *Il **n'y a pas de** cinéma* ('There isn't a cinema'). *Il y a une piscine* becomes *Il n'y a pas de piscine*. *Il y a des magasins* becomes *Il n'y a pas de magasins*. And before a vowel: *Il n'y a pas d'église*.
## Saying where things are

To give directions or describe where things are, use: *à côté de* (next to), *en face de* (opposite), *près de* (near), *loin de* (far from) and *au centre-ville* (in the town centre). For example: *La bibliothèque est en face de la gare* ('The library is opposite the station').
## Giving your opinion

To get top marks, always add an opinion and a reason. You can describe your town with **C'est…** ('It's…'): *animé* (lively), *calme* (quiet), *joli* (pretty), *moderne* (modern), *historique* (historic), *ennuyeux* (boring) or *sale* (dirty). Use **parce que** ('because') to give a reason: *J'aime ma ville parce que c'est animé et il y a beaucoup de magasins* ('I like my town because it's lively and there are lots of shops'). Or be more critical: *Je n'aime pas ma ville parce qu'il n'y a pas de cinéma. C'est un peu ennuyeux pour les jeunes* ('I don't like my town because there isn't a cinema. It's a bit boring for young people').
## Putting it all together

Here's a short answer that would impress any French teacher: *J'habite à Bristol. C'est une grande ville historique. Il y a un musée, un stade et beaucoup de magasins, mais il n'y a pas de patinoire. J'aime aller au café avec mes amis. D'habitude, je prends un chocolat chaud et une crêpe !* Notice how it uses *il y a*, *il n'y a pas de*, an opinion and a connective. That's the formula: **what there is, what there isn't, and what you think**.

The bill, please
There is… / There are…
There isn't / aren't any… (un/une/des become de after a negative)
'a' — un for masculine nouns, une for feminine nouns

questions.q: What is the most polite way to order a hot chocolate?
options: Je voudrais un chocolat chaud, s'il vous plaît.
questions.explain: Je voudrais… s'il vous plaît ('I would like… please') is polite. 'Donne-moi' means 'give me', and 'Tu veux…?' means 'Do you want…?' — both wrong for ordering.

questions.q: What does 'L'addition, s'il vous plaît' mean?
questions.explain: L'addition is the bill. A useful link: you 'add up' what you owe.

questions.q: Which is correct?
questions.explain: Limonade is feminine, so it's une limonade. The others should be un café, une crêpe and une piscine. Learn each noun with its un or une.

questions.q: What does 'Il y a' mean?
questions.explain: Il y a means 'there is' or 'there are': Il y a un parc (there is a park), il y a des magasins (there are some shops).

questions.q: How do you say 'There isn't a swimming pool'?
options: Il n'y a pas une piscine
Il n'y a une piscine pas
Il n'y a pas de piscine
questions.explain: After a negative (ne… pas), un/une/des change to de. So it's il n'y a pas de piscine — not 'pas une piscine'.

questions.q: What is 'une bibliothèque'?
questions.explain: Une bibliothèque is a library. Watch out: a bookshop is une librairie — a classic 'false friend'.

questions.q: Why should you use 'vous' rather than 'tu' with a waiter?
options: Vous is the polite form, used with adults you don't know
Tu is only used in writing
Tu is only for talking about food
questions.explain: Vous is polite (and also plural). Tu is for friends, family, children and pets. Using tu with a waiter can sound rude.

questions.q: 'La bibliothèque est en face de la gare.' Where is the library?
questions.explain: En face de means 'opposite'. Next to is à côté de, and far from is loin de.

questions.q: Which sentence includes an opinion and a reason?
options: J'aime ma ville parce que c'est animé.
Il n'y a pas de cinéma.
questions.explain: J'aime… parce que c'est animé ('I like… because it's lively') gives an opinion (j'aime) and a reason (parce que…). Adding opinions and reasons is how to reach higher marks.

questions.q: You order un café (€2.50) and un croissant (€1.50). The waiter says 'Ça fait quatre euros.' Is that right?
options: No — it should be quatorze euros
No — it should be trois euros
No — it should be cinq euros
questions.explain: Quatre = 4, and €2.50 + €1.50 = €4.00. (Quatorze is 14, trois is 3 and cinq is 5.)

In English, explain the rule for what happens to un, une and des after 'il n'y a pas', and give an example.

sessions.subject: PRE
sessions.topic: Is it rational to believe in God?

read.title: Is it rational to believe in God?
read.intro: One of the oldest questions people have asked. This isn't about who's right — it's about weighing up the arguments.
body: Billions of people around the world believe in God, and billions do not. Thoughtful, intelligent people are found on both sides. Philosophers have argued about God's existence for thousands of years, and the debate is still going. In PRE, the aim is not to tell you what to believe. It is to understand the arguments, weigh them up, and be able to explain your own view and the views of people who disagree with you.
## What does 'rational' mean?

To be **rational** means to base your beliefs on **reasons**: logic and evidence. So the question is not 'Is God real?' — which nobody can prove either way — but 'Are there good reasons to believe in God, or good reasons not to?'

It helps to know some key words. A **theist** believes in God. An **atheist** believes there is no God. An **agnostic** believes we cannot know whether God exists — the word was invented by the biologist Thomas Huxley, a friend of Darwin, in 1869. The God most often discussed in these arguments is the God of Christianity, Judaism and Islam: all-powerful (**omnipotent**), all-knowing (**omniscient**), all-loving (**omnibenevolent**), and the creator of the universe.
## Argument 1: the first cause

Everything we see has a cause. You exist because of your parents; a tree exists because of a seed. But what caused the universe? If every cause has a cause before it, you get a never-ending chain going back for ever. Many philosophers find that idea impossible. So, the argument goes, there must have been a **first cause** that was not itself caused — and that, believers say, is God. This is called the **cosmological argument**. One famous version was written by **Thomas Aquinas**, an Italian monk and philosopher, in the 13th century.

Some believers point out that science supports part of this. The **Big Bang theory** says the universe had a beginning around 13.8 billion years ago. Interestingly, the scientist who first proposed it, **Georges Lemaître**, was a Catholic priest.

Critics reply with a simple question: if everything needs a cause, **what caused God?** If believers say God doesn't need a cause, why can't the universe itself just exist without one? Others argue that just because things *inside* the universe have causes, we can't be sure the universe as a whole needs one.
## Argument 2: design

In 1802, an English clergyman called **William Paley** asked his readers to imagine finding a watch lying on the ground. Unlike a stone, its parts fit together so precisely for a purpose — telling the time — that you would conclude it had a designer. Paley argued that living things, such as the human eye, are far more complex than any watch, so they must have a designer too: God. This is the **design argument** (or **teleological argument**). Some modern believers add that the laws of physics seem 'fine-tuned' for life: if gravity were slightly stronger or weaker, stars and planets could never have formed.

The biggest challenge to Paley came from science — you'll meet it properly in this afternoon's session. **Darwin's theory of natural selection** explains how complex living things can develop gradually, without anyone designing them, through small changes over millions of years. Critics also point out that nature contains things that seem badly designed — and a great deal of suffering. Some believers respond that God could have *used* evolution as a way of creating, so there's no contradiction between science and faith.
## Argument 3: religious experience

Many people say they have experienced God directly: through prayer, through a sense of overwhelming peace, or through a life-changing moment, such as Saul's conversion on the road to Damascus in the Bible. For believers, this is powerful personal evidence. If you trust your experience that a table is in front of you, why not trust your experience of God?

Critics say experiences can be explained in other ways — tiredness, emotion, the power of suggestion, or even brain chemistry — and that people of different religions experience very different things, which makes it hard to know which, if any, is real.
## Argument against: evil and suffering

The strongest argument against God's existence for many people is the **problem of evil**. It goes back to the ancient Greek philosopher **Epicurus**. If God is all-powerful, God could stop suffering. If God is all-loving, God would want to stop suffering. Yet suffering exists: children die of disease, earthquakes kill thousands. So, the argument says, an all-powerful, all-loving God cannot exist.

Believers have several replies. One is **free will**: God gave humans the freedom to choose, and much suffering comes from humans choosing to do wrong. Another is that suffering can help people develop courage, compassion and patience. Others say that humans are simply too limited to understand God's reasons. Critics answer that free will doesn't explain natural disasters or disease.
## Faith and reason

Some believers say the whole question misses the point. For them, belief in God is a matter of **faith**: trust that goes beyond what can be proved. The 19th-century Danish philosopher **Søren Kierkegaard** called it a 'leap of faith'. The French mathematician **Blaise Pascal** argued that believing is a sensible bet: if God exists, believers gain everything; if not, they lose very little. Critics reply that you can't simply choose to believe something, and that faith without evidence could justify believing anything at all. The philosopher **Bertrand Russell** made this point with his imaginary teapot orbiting the Sun — too small to be seen with any telescope. You can't disprove it, he said, but that doesn't make it reasonable to believe in it.
## Where does that leave us?

In the 2021 census, 46% of people in England and Wales described themselves as Christian and 37% said they had no religion — up from 25% ten years earlier. Belief is changing, but the arguments remain. A strong PRE answer doesn't just give one side: it explains the arguments **for** and **against**, evaluates how convincing each is, and reaches a reasoned conclusion of its own.

keywords.def: Based on reasons — logic and evidence.
Believes in God / believes there is no God / believes we can't know.
The universe must have a first cause, which is God.
The complexity and order of the world suggest a designer, which is God (e.g. Paley's watch).
If God is all-powerful and all-loving, why does suffering exist?
Trust or belief that goes beyond what can be proved.

questions.q: What does it mean for a belief to be 'rational'?
options: It is based on reasons: logic and evidence
It is believed by most people
It comes from a religious book
questions.explain: A rational belief is backed by reasons. You can hold a rational belief that later turns out wrong — the question is whether the reasons are good.

questions.q: What is an agnostic?
options: Someone who believes in many gods
Someone who believes there is no God
Someone who believes we cannot know whether God exists
questions.explain: An agnostic says we can't know either way. An atheist believes there is no God. The word 'agnostic' was coined by Thomas Huxley in 1869.

questions.q: Which argument says the universe needs a first cause?
questions.explain: The cosmological argument (from 'cosmos', the universe) says the chain of causes must start somewhere, with an uncaused cause — God.

questions.q: What was William Paley's watch analogy trying to show?
options: That watches were invented by God
That complex things with a purpose suggest a designer
That time began with the Big Bang
questions.explain: If a watch's complex, purposeful design implies a watchmaker, Paley argued, then the far more complex natural world implies a designer: God.

questions.q: How does Darwin's theory of natural selection challenge the design argument?
options: It explains how complex living things can develop gradually without a designer
It proves God does not exist
It shows the universe has no beginning
questions.explain: Natural selection offers another explanation for complexity, so design isn't the only possibility. It doesn't disprove God — some believers think God works through evolution.

questions.q: What is the problem of evil?
options: Religions disagree about what evil is
If God is all-powerful and all-loving, it's hard to explain why suffering exists
questions.explain: The problem goes back to Epicurus: a God who could stop suffering and wanted to would stop it — yet suffering exists.

questions.q: Which is a believer's response to the problem of evil?
options: God gave humans free will, and much suffering comes from human choices
questions.explain: The free will defence says a world with real choice must allow people to choose wrongly. Critics reply that it doesn't explain earthquakes or disease.

questions.q: What is a weakness of the cosmological argument?
options: It was written too long ago
If everything needs a cause, it raises the question of what caused God
questions.explain: If believers say God needs no cause, critics ask why the universe couldn't also exist without one. That's the main challenge to a first-cause argument.

questions.q: What point was Bertrand Russell making with his imaginary teapot orbiting the Sun?
options: Teapots are a good example of design
Something that can't be disproved isn't automatically reasonable to believe
questions.explain: You can't disprove a tiny invisible teapot, but that's no reason to believe in it. Russell argued the burden of proof lies with the person making the claim.

questions.q: In England and Wales, 'no religion' rose from about 25% in 2011 to about 37% in 2021. By how many percentage points did it rise?
questions.explain: 37 − 25 = 12 percentage points. (62 would be adding them, and 1.5 is roughly how many times larger 37 is than 25.)

reflect: Choose one argument for God's existence and one argument against. Explain each in your own words.
Can someone be rational and still have faith? Give your own view with a reason, then explain how someone might disagree.

sessions.subject: Science

read.title: Darwin's big idea: evolution by natural selection
read.intro: How a five-year voyage, some finches and a lot of patient thinking changed how we see all life on Earth.
body: In 1831, a 22-year-old Englishman called **Charles Darwin** set sail on a ship called HMS *Beagle*. He had not long left university, where he had trained to become a clergyman, but what he really loved was collecting beetles, rocks and fossils. The *Beagle*'s job was to map the coastline of South America, and Darwin went along as a naturalist. The voyage lasted almost five years. The ideas it gave him took more than twenty years to publish, and they changed science for ever.
## The puzzle of the Galápagos

In 1835 the *Beagle* reached the **Galápagos Islands**, a group of volcanic islands in the Pacific Ocean, about 1,000 km off the coast of Ecuador. Darwin noticed something odd. Each island had its own slightly different types of animals. The giant tortoises on one island had different-shaped shells from those on another. There were mockingbirds that differed from island to island. And there were many kinds of small birds — later known as **Darwin's finches** — with beaks of very different shapes and sizes.

Some finches had big, strong beaks, like nutcrackers, which were good for cracking hard seeds. Others had thin, pointed beaks, ideal for catching insects or probing flowers. Each beak seemed perfectly suited to the food available on that bird's island. These are examples of **adaptations**: features that help an organism survive in its environment.

Back in England, Darwin puzzled over why. At the time, most people believed that every species had been created separately in its present form and had never changed. But if that were true, why would each small island have its own slightly different version of a finch? Darwin began to suspect that the finches had all descended from a few birds that had arrived from South America long ago, and had gradually changed to suit each island.
## The idea of natural selection
Darwin's explanation is called **natural selection**. It rests on a few simple observations that anyone can check.

**1. Variation.** Individuals of the same species are not identical. Some finches have slightly bigger beaks than others; some rabbits run slightly faster; some plants survive frost better. Much of this variation is passed on from parents to offspring — today we know it is carried in genes, and that it comes from meiosis and fertilisation, which you learned about this week.

**2. Too many offspring.** Living things produce far more young than can possibly survive. A single cod can lay millions of eggs; a pair of rabbits can have dozens of babies a year. If they all survived, the world would soon be overrun.
**3. Competition.** So there is a **struggle for survival**. Individuals compete for food, water, space and mates, and many die from predators or disease before they can breed.

**4. Survival of the best adapted.** Individuals whose variations make them slightly better suited to their environment are more likely to survive. A finch with a beak that cracks seeds a little more easily gets more food in a hard year.
**5. Passing it on.** The survivors breed and pass on their useful characteristics to their offspring.

**6. Change over time.** Over many generations, the useful characteristics become more common in the population. The species gradually changes. This is **evolution**. Given enough time and enough change, a population may become so different that it forms a **new species**.

The phrase 'survival of the fittest' is often used for this, but 'fittest' does not mean the strongest or the most athletic. It means the best **fitted**, or suited, to the environment. In a snowy landscape, a white rabbit that is hard for foxes to spot may be 'fittest', even if it is smaller and slower than a brown one.
## A common mistake

Before Darwin, a French scientist called **Jean-Baptiste Lamarck** suggested that animals change during their own lives and pass those changes on. He thought giraffes got long necks by stretching to reach high leaves, and then had babies with slightly longer necks. We now know this is wrong. Stretching your neck doesn't change your genes, just as a weightlifter's big muscles don't get passed on to their children. In Darwin's explanation, giraffes born with slightly longer necks, by chance, could reach more food, survived better and had more young. The change happens in the **population** over generations, not in an individual during its life. Individuals don't evolve; populations do.
## Darwin goes public

Darwin knew his idea would be controversial, because it challenged the belief that all species had been created as they are. He spent years gathering evidence. Then, in 1858, he received a letter from another naturalist, **Alfred Russel Wallace**, who was working in South-East Asia and had come up with almost exactly the same idea. Their work was presented together that year, and in 1859 Darwin published his famous book, *On the Origin of Species*. It caused a sensation. Some religious leaders attacked it, while others came to accept it. Darwin carefully avoided saying much about humans in that book, but his later work argued that humans, too, had evolved.
## Evolution in action

You might think evolution is too slow to watch, but sometimes it can be measured. In the 1970s, two scientists, **Peter and Rosemary Grant**, studied finches on a tiny Galápagos island called Daphne Major. In 1977, a severe drought killed most of the plants, leaving mainly large, hard seeds. Most of the finches died. The survivors were mostly birds with larger, deeper beaks, which could crack the tough seeds. When they bred, their chicks had larger beaks on average than the population before the drought. The Grants had watched natural selection change a population in a single generation.
## Why it matters

Evolution by natural selection is one of the most important ideas in science. It explains why living things are so well suited to their environments, why species are related to each other, and how life has changed over billions of years — from simple single cells to the millions of species alive today. It is also why scientists worry about bacteria becoming resistant to antibiotics, which you will meet in Friday's session on the evidence for evolution.

keywords.def: The gradual change in the characteristics of a species over many generations.
The process where individuals best suited to their environment survive, breed and pass on their characteristics.
A feature that helps an organism survive in its environment, e.g. a seed-cracking beak.
A group of organisms that can breed together to produce fertile offspring.
When organisms struggle for the same limited resources, such as food, water, space or mates.
Naturalist (1809–1882) who explained evolution by natural selection in On the Origin of Species (1859).

questions.q: Which islands did Darwin visit where he noticed finches with different beaks?
questions.explain: The Galápagos Islands, in the Pacific off Ecuador. Each island had its own varieties of finch, tortoise and mockingbird.

questions.q: What is an adaptation?
options: A feature that helps an organism survive in its environment
A change an animal makes during its life by practising
A disease that kills a species
questions.explain: Adaptations are inherited features that suit an organism to its environment, like a nutcracker beak for hard seeds or white fur in snow.

questions.q: In natural selection, what does 'survival of the fittest' really mean?
options: The strongest animals always win fights
Individuals best suited to their environment are most likely to survive and breed
questions.explain: 'Fittest' means best fitted to the environment. A small white rabbit in the snow may be fitter than a big brown one, because foxes can't see it as easily.

questions.q: Who came up with the idea of natural selection at the same time as Darwin?
questions.explain: Wallace independently reached the same idea, and their work was presented together in 1858. Lamarck had an earlier, incorrect theory.

questions.q: Why is variation essential for natural selection?
options: Without variation, all animals would be the same colour
If all individuals were identical, none would be better suited than others, so nothing could be 'selected'
questions.explain: Natural selection works by some individuals surviving better than others. That's only possible if they differ. This is where meiosis comes in: it creates the variation that selection acts on.

questions.q: Lamarck said giraffes got long necks by stretching. What is wrong with this idea?
options: Changes made during an animal's life don't change its genes, so they aren't passed on
questions.explain: Stretching doesn't alter genes, just as a weightlifter's muscles aren't inherited. Instead, giraffes born with slightly longer necks survived better and passed that feature on.

questions.q: Rabbits in a snowy area vary in fur colour. Foxes hunt them. What would you expect after many generations?
options: The rabbits will choose to grow white fur
The proportion of white-furred rabbits will increase
All the rabbits will become brown
questions.explain: White rabbits are harder to spot, so more survive to breed and pass on white fur. Over generations, white fur becomes more common. The rabbits don't choose anything — survival does the selecting.

questions.q: What happened to Darwin's finches on Daphne Major after the 1977 drought?
options: They all moved to another island
The average beak size of the next generation got larger
Their beaks stretched while they were eating
questions.explain: Only large, hard seeds were left, so birds with bigger beaks survived and bred. Their chicks inherited bigger beaks, so the average went up — natural selection seen in one generation.

questions.q: Which sentence about evolution is correct?
options: An individual animal evolves during its lifetime
Animals evolve because they want to
Evolution only happened in the past
questions.explain: Individuals don't evolve; populations do, as the proportions of different characteristics change over generations. And evolution is still happening — the Grants' finches show that.

questions.q: Darwin visited the Galápagos in 1835 and published On the Origin of Species in 1859. How long did he wait?
questions.explain: 1859 − 1835 = 24 years. Darwin spent those years collecting evidence because he knew his idea would be challenged.

reflect: Explain the steps of natural selection using your own made-up example (for example, beetles, birds or plants). Use the words 'variation', 'survive' and 'pass on'.
Explain why a giraffe stretching its neck does not give its babies longer necks, and what really happened instead.
