sessions.topic: The Amazon: why it's being cleared

read.title: The Amazon: a rainforest under pressure
read.intro: Why is the world's largest rainforest being cut down — and who gets to decide what happens to it?
body: The Amazon is the largest tropical rainforest on Earth. It covers about 5.5 million square kilometres — more than twenty times the size of the UK — and about 60% of it lies in Brazil. It is home to around one in ten of all the known species of plants and animals on the planet, including jaguars, sloths, pink river dolphins and more than 16,000 species of tree. Hundreds of indigenous groups live there, some of whom have had almost no contact with the outside world. Yet every year, large areas of the forest are cut down. To understand why, you have to look at it from several points of view.
## Why the rainforest matters

You may have heard the Amazon called 'the lungs of the world', and the claim that it produces 20% of the world's oxygen. That's actually a myth: the forest uses up almost as much oxygen as it makes, as plants and animals respire and dead material rots. But the Amazon is vitally important for other reasons.

First, it is a huge **carbon store**. Its trees hold an enormous amount of carbon. When the forest is cut down and burned, that carbon is released into the air as carbon dioxide, adding to **climate change**.

Second, it makes its own rain. Trees draw water up from the soil and release it from their leaves, a process called **transpiration**. This moisture forms clouds that drop rain further across the forest — and huge 'flying rivers' of water vapour carry rain far to the south, to the farms and cities of southern Brazil. Fewer trees means less rain, both in the forest and beyond it.
Third, its **biodiversity** — the variety of life — is extraordinary. Many medicines have come from rainforest plants, and scientists believe there are countless species still undiscovered.
## How much has been lost?

Since 1970, around a fifth of Brazil's Amazon rainforest has been cleared. The rate of clearance has risen and fallen over time. In 2004, about 27,800 km² was cleared in a single year — an area larger than Wales. Strong action by the government then cut the rate dramatically, to about 4,600 km² in 2012. It rose again in the late 2010s, before falling sharply once more after 2023. Scientists use satellites to measure the loss each year, so these figures are carefully monitored.
## Why is it being cut down?

**Cattle ranching** is the biggest cause. Most cleared land is turned into pasture for beef cattle. Brazil is one of the world's largest beef exporters, and ranchers can make money quickly by clearing land and grazing animals on it.

**Commercial farming**, especially of **soya beans**, is another major cause. Brazil is the world's biggest exporter of soya, much of which is used to feed animals such as chickens and pigs in other countries, including the UK.

**Logging** removes valuable hardwood trees, such as mahogany, for furniture and building. Some logging is legal, but a great deal is illegal. Logging roads then open up the forest to settlers and ranchers.

**Mining** brings jobs and wealth. Carajás, in the Brazilian Amazon, is one of the largest iron ore mines in the world. Illegal gold miners have also invaded the forest and indigenous lands, using mercury that poisons rivers and the fish that local people eat.
**Roads** such as the Trans-Amazonian Highway, begun in the 1970s, cut deep into the forest. Wherever a road goes, settlers, loggers and farmers follow, clearing land on either side.

**Energy** projects also play a part. Brazil has built huge **hydroelectric dams** on Amazon rivers, such as Belo Monte, to generate electricity. They provide renewable energy for millions of people, but they flood large areas of forest and force people from their homes.
## The effects

Deforestation has serious effects. **Biodiversity** is lost as habitats are destroyed, and some species may become extinct before they are even discovered. **Climate change** is made worse by the carbon released. Rainforest soils are surprisingly thin and poor: most nutrients are held in the living plants, not the ground. Once the trees are removed, heavy rain washes the remaining nutrients away, a process called **leaching**, and the soil erodes. So cleared land often becomes unproductive within a few years, and farmers clear more forest. **Indigenous peoples** lose their land, their way of life and sometimes their lives in conflicts with loggers and miners.

Some scientists warn of a **tipping point**. If too much forest is lost — perhaps 20–25% — the remaining forest might not be able to make enough of its own rain, and large parts could dry out and turn into savanna grassland.
## Different points of view

This is where geography gets complicated. For a poor farming family, clearing a patch of forest might be the only way to grow food and earn money. For the Brazilian government, farming, mining and energy create jobs, pay for schools and hospitals, and help the country develop. Many Brazilians also point out that rich countries like the UK cut down most of their own forests centuries ago — by the early 1900s, only about 5% of Britain was woodland — so why should Brazil be told not to do the same? For indigenous people, the forest is home. For the rest of the world, its effect on the climate makes it everyone's business.
## Protecting the forest

There are ways to protect the Amazon while still allowing people to earn a living. Brazil has created large **protected areas** and **indigenous reserves**, where clearing is banned; studies show they slow deforestation. **Satellite monitoring** can spot illegal clearing within days. Since 2006, big soya traders have agreed not to buy soya grown on newly cleared rainforest. Other countries, such as Norway and Germany, have paid into an **Amazon Fund** to reward Brazil for reducing deforestation. **Sustainable** activities, such as harvesting Brazil nuts, açaí berries and rubber, and **ecotourism**, can make the forest worth more standing than cut down. In 2025, Brazil hosted the United Nations climate conference, COP30, in the Amazon city of Belém, putting the forest at the centre of world attention.
Whether these efforts succeed will depend on choices made by governments, companies and consumers — including the people who buy beef, soya and furniture in countries thousands of miles away.

keywords.def: Cutting down or clearing large areas of forest.
The variety of plant and animal life in an area.
Something that holds carbon, keeping it out of the atmosphere, e.g. trees.
Water moving up through a plant and evaporating from its leaves.
When rain washes nutrients out of the soil.
Meeting people's needs today without damaging the ability of future generations to meet theirs.

questions.q: What is the biggest cause of deforestation in the Amazon?
questions.explain: Most cleared land in the Amazon becomes pasture for beef cattle. Soya farming, logging and mining are also major causes.

questions.q: Is it true that the Amazon produces 20% of the world's oxygen?
options: Yes, it produces all the world's oxygen
No — it's a myth, because the forest uses almost as much oxygen as it makes
No — rainforests don't produce any oxygen
questions.explain: The forest does produce oxygen by photosynthesis, but plants, animals and decay use almost all of it. The Amazon's real global importance is as a carbon store and rain-maker.

questions.q: Why does cutting down the Amazon add to climate change?
options: Carbon stored in the trees is released as carbon dioxide when they are burned or rot
questions.explain: The trees are a huge carbon store. Burning or rotting releases that carbon as CO₂, a greenhouse gas.

questions.q: Why does cleared rainforest land often become poor for farming within a few years?
options: It is too cold for crops
Farmers are not allowed to use it
The soil is thin, and heavy rain washes the nutrients away (leaching)
questions.explain: Most nutrients are in the living plants, not the soil. Once the trees go, rain leaches nutrients away, so farmers often clear more forest.

questions.q: How do roads such as the Trans-Amazonian Highway increase deforestation?
options: They open up the forest to settlers, loggers and farmers
questions.explain: Roads give access. Once a road is built, people follow it into the forest and clear land on either side.

questions.q: Why might the Brazilian government support some development in the Amazon?
options: Because it creates jobs and money that help the country develop
Because the UK told them to
questions.explain: Farming, mining and energy bring jobs and tax income for schools and hospitals. Good answers recognise that different groups have different, often reasonable, points of view.

questions.q: Which of these is a sustainable way to use the rainforest?
options: Harvesting Brazil nuts and açaí berries
Burning trees to make space for soya
questions.explain: Harvesting nuts and fruit earns money while leaving the forest standing, so it can continue for generations.

questions.q: What is meant by a 'tipping point' for the Amazon?
options: The point where tourists stop visiting
The point where the forest is fully protected
The highest point in the Amazon
If too much forest is lost, the rest may not make enough rain and could turn to savanna
questions.explain: The forest helps make its own rain. Lose too much, and the remaining forest could dry out — a change that might be impossible to reverse.

questions.q: Deforestation was about 27,800 km² in 2004 and about 4,600 km² in 2012. Roughly what fraction of the 2004 rate was the 2012 rate?
questions.explain: 4,600 ÷ 27,800 ≈ 0.17, which is about 1/6. In other words, the yearly loss fell by more than four-fifths.

questions.q: The Amazon covers about 5.5 million km². About 60% is in Brazil. Roughly how much is that?
questions.explain: 60% of 5.5 million = 0.6 × 5.5 = 3.3 million km². A quick way: 10% is 0.55, so 60% is 6 × 0.55 = 3.3.

reflect: Explain two reasons why the Amazon is being cleared, and why each matters to the people doing the clearing.
Should Brazil be allowed to use its rainforest to grow richer, as the UK did with its forests long ago? Give both sides, then your own view.

sessions.subject: Science

read.title: How do we know evolution happened?
read.intro: Fossils, moths and superbugs: the evidence that convinced scientists — and how you can see evolution happening today.
body: A good scientific theory needs evidence. When Darwin published *On the Origin of Species* in 1859, many people asked: how can you prove that species change over millions of years, if nobody was there to see it? Since then, scientists have collected evidence from rocks, from living animals, from history and even from inside our own cells. Together, it makes evolution one of the best-supported ideas in all of science.
## Evidence 1: fossils

**Fossils** are the remains or traces of living things from long ago, preserved in rock. They form when an organism is buried quickly, for example in mud at the bottom of a lake or sea. Over thousands of years, the hard parts, such as bones, shells and teeth, are slowly replaced by minerals, turning them to stone. Footprints, burrows and even fossilised dung can be preserved too.

Rocks are laid down in layers, with the oldest at the bottom. When scientists study the fossils in each layer, they see a clear pattern. The deepest, oldest rocks contain only simple life, like bacteria. Higher up come simple sea creatures, then fish, then animals that lived on land, and finally mammals and birds. Humans appear only in the very latest layers. This order is exactly what evolution predicts.

Some of the most exciting fossils are **transitional fossils**, which show features of two different groups. **Archaeopteryx**, found in Germany in 1861, just two years after Darwin's book, had feathers and wings like a bird, but also teeth, claws and a long bony tail like a small dinosaur. In 2004, scientists in the Canadian Arctic discovered **Tiktaalik**, a 375-million-year-old fish with a neck, strong fins with wrist-like bones, and lungs — a creature halfway between fish and land animals.

Britain played a big part in fossil hunting. In the early 1800s, **Mary Anning**, a young woman from Lyme Regis in Dorset, found spectacular fossils of ancient sea reptiles, such as ichthyosaurs, in the cliffs. Because she was a woman from a poor family, scientists of the time often failed to give her credit, but today she is recognised as one of the most important fossil hunters in history.

The fossil record isn't complete. Most living things never become fossils: soft bodies decay quickly, and the right conditions are rare. Many fossils have also been destroyed by movements of the Earth's crust, or simply haven't been found yet. That's why there are gaps — but every new fossil discovered has fitted the pattern.
## Evidence 2: similar body plans

Look at your own arm: one bone in the upper arm, two in the forearm, a cluster of wrist bones, and five fingers. Now look at the skeleton of a bat's wing, a whale's flipper, a bird's wing or a cat's front leg. They are used for flying, swimming and walking, yet they all have the same basic pattern of bones. Scientists call this the **pentadactyl limb** ('five-fingered limb'). The simplest explanation is that all these animals evolved from a shared ancestor that had this limb, and it was gradually adapted in different ways.
## Evidence 3: DNA

Since the discovery of the structure of DNA in 1953, scientists have been able to compare the genes of different species. The more closely related two species are, the more similar their DNA. Humans and chimpanzees share about 98–99% of their DNA, which shows that they share a recent common ancestor — not that humans are descended from chimps, but that both evolved from the same ancestor, around 6 to 7 million years ago. Humans share less DNA with mice, less again with fish, and less still with plants. These patterns match the 'family tree' that fossils show.
## Evidence 4: the peppered moth

Peppered moths live in Britain. Most were once pale with dark speckles, which camouflaged them on pale, lichen-covered tree trunks. A rare dark form also existed. During the **Industrial Revolution**, smoke and soot from factories killed the lichens and blackened tree trunks around cities like Manchester. Now the pale moths stood out, and birds ate them. The dark moths were camouflaged and survived. By the late 1800s, almost all the peppered moths around Manchester were dark.

In the 1950s, the scientist **Bernard Kettlewell** tested this by releasing moths and recording which ones birds caught. Then, after laws such as the **Clean Air Act of 1956** reduced pollution, the trees became paler again — and the pale form became common once more. It is a clear case of natural selection, happening in Britain within a human lifetime.
## Evidence 5: antibiotic resistance

The most worrying example of evolution today is happening in hospitals. **Antibiotics** are medicines that kill bacteria. But bacteria reproduce incredibly fast — in ideal conditions, some can divide every 20 minutes — and their DNA sometimes changes at random. These changes are called **mutations**. Very occasionally, a mutation makes a bacterium **resistant** to an antibiotic.

When a patient takes an antibiotic, it kills the non-resistant bacteria. The resistant ones survive, reproduce and pass on their resistance. Soon, a whole population of resistant bacteria can exist, and the antibiotic no longer works. **MRSA**, a 'superbug' resistant to several common antibiotics, evolved this way. This is natural selection in action, and it's why doctors don't prescribe antibiotics for colds (which are caused by viruses, not bacteria), and why patients are told to finish the full course.
## Putting it together

Each piece of evidence on its own is interesting. Together, they are powerful: fossils show change over time in the right order; body plans and DNA show species are related; and peppered moths and superbugs show natural selection happening right now. That's why evolution is accepted by scientists across the world, including many who are religious. As you saw in PRE, the arguments about what evolution means for belief in God continue — but the evidence that species evolve is overwhelming.

keywords.def: The preserved remains or traces of an organism from long ago, usually in rock.
A fossil showing features of two different groups, e.g. Archaeopteryx (dinosaur and bird).
A limb with a five-digit bone pattern, shared by many vertebrates, e.g. human arms and bat wings.
A random change in DNA. Mutations create new variation.
A medicine that kills bacteria (but not viruses).
Not affected by something, e.g. bacteria that an antibiotic can no longer kill.

questions.q: Why do the oldest rocks contain only simple life forms?
options: Simple organisms were the only life that existed when those rocks formed
Complex animals sank to the bottom
The oldest rocks are too hot for complex life
questions.explain: Rock layers build up over time, so deeper layers are older. Simple life appears first, then more complex life — exactly the order evolution predicts.

questions.q: What made Archaeopteryx such an important fossil?
options: It was the first fossil ever found
It showed features of both dinosaurs and birds
It was a fossil of a human
questions.explain: Archaeopteryx had feathers and wings like a bird, but teeth, claws and a bony tail like a dinosaur — a transitional fossil linking two groups.

questions.q: Why are there gaps in the fossil record?
options: Animals didn't exist at certain times
Most organisms never fossilise, and many fossils have been destroyed or not yet found
questions.explain: Fossilisation needs rare conditions, soft parts usually decay, and Earth movements destroy rocks. So the record is incomplete — but new finds keep fitting the pattern.

questions.q: Human arms, bat wings and whale flippers have the same basic bone pattern. What does this suggest?
options: They all evolved from a shared ancestor
They are all used for flying
questions.explain: The same pentadactyl pattern, adapted for different jobs, is best explained by a common ancestor. Humans didn't evolve from bats; both evolved from an older shared ancestor.

questions.q: Humans share about 98–99% of their DNA with chimpanzees. What does this show?
options: Humans are descended from modern chimpanzees
Humans and chimpanzees share a recent common ancestor
DNA is the same in all living things
questions.explain: Similar DNA means close relationship. Humans and chimps both evolved from a common ancestor about 6–7 million years ago — modern chimps aren't our ancestors.

questions.q: Why did dark peppered moths become common near Manchester during the Industrial Revolution?
options: The soot dyed the moths black
Pale moths moved away to the countryside
Dark moths were better camouflaged on sooty trees, so fewer were eaten by birds
questions.explain: Soot darkened the trees. Dark moths were harder for birds to see, so they survived and bred more, passing on the dark colour. The soot didn't change the moths' genes — that would be Lamarck's mistake.

questions.q: What happened to peppered moths after the Clean Air Act of 1956 reduced pollution?
options: The pale form became common again
questions.explain: As trees became paler again, the pale moths were camouflaged and the dark ones stood out, so selection reversed. That's strong evidence that the environment drives the change.

questions.q: Put these in order to show how antibiotic resistance develops: (1) resistant bacteria survive and reproduce; (2) a random mutation makes one bacterium resistant; (3) the antibiotic kills non-resistant bacteria.
questions.explain: First a mutation creates resistance (2), then the antibiotic kills the others (3), leaving the resistant ones to multiply (1). Variation, selection, then inheritance.

questions.q: Why shouldn't doctors prescribe antibiotics for a cold?
options: Colds are caused by viruses, which antibiotics don't kill
Colds are caused by bacteria that are always resistant
questions.explain: Antibiotics kill bacteria, not viruses. Using them when they can't help just gives bacteria in your body more chances to evolve resistance.

questions.q: A bacterium divides every 20 minutes, and every new cell keeps dividing. Starting with one bacterium, how many will there be after 2 hours?
questions.explain: 2 hours = 120 minutes = 6 divisions. The number doubles each time: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 → 16 → 32 → 64. That speed is why resistance can spread so quickly.
